description:
I'm a passionate computer science student participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge. I'm interested in software development, AI, web technologies, and space exploration. Currently, I'm working on an astronaut health monitoring system to support crew safety and well-being. I enjoy problem-solving, learning new technologies, and turning creative ideas into practical solutions.

I'm looking for motivated, creative, and collaborative teammates with skills in AI/ML, Python, web development, UI/.
summary:
Our project, Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions, aims to develop an intelligent digital health monitoring system designed to support astronaut safety and well-being during space exploration. Space missions expose astronauts to challenging conditions, including microgravity, isolation, radiation, and limited access to medical facilities. These factors can significantly affect their physical health and overall performance.
Our proposed software will continuously monitor important health indicators such as heart rate, body temperature, blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂), blood pressure, and other vital signs. The system will analyze collected health data, identify unusual changes, and generate real-time alerts whenever an astronaut's health indicators move outside predefined safe ranges.
The platform will provide an easy-to-use dashboard displaying individual health records, live monitoring information, health trends, and emergency notifications. It will also help mission control teams observe astronauts' health conditions remotely and make informed decisions when medical attention is required.
By integrating data analysis, intelligent monitoring, and visualization, our solution aims to reduce health-related risks and improve medical support during long-duration space missions. It is designed with future scalability in mind, allowing additional monitoring devices and analytical features to be integrated.
details:
Astro Health Companion is a self-assessment tool that lets an astronaut record their own health indicators during a long-duration mission, understand what each reading means, and decide what to do next.

An astronaut logs a measurement: systolic and diastolic blood pressure, resting heart rate, blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂), blood glucose, body temperature, sleep, or mood. The app checks the value immediately against reference ranges and returns three things: a status (within range, caution, or critical), a plain-language message, and a specific next step. A critical result says to stop exertion and contact the flight surgeon. A caution result says what to rest, drink, or recheck.

The app also works over time:

  • Trends chart each indicator against its reference band, with every reading coloured by status.
  • Escalation raises a “notify the flight surgeon” notice when three readings in a row fall outside range, so a slow drift is caught even when no single value looks alarming.
  • Body map links the body’s systems (heart, lungs, glucose metabolism, brain, muscles and bones) to the measurements that check them, and explains what each one does in space.
  • Daily routine prompts the measurements and exercise that a mission protocol calls for. Logging a reading completes its task automatically.
  • Learn explains each measurement: what it is, why spaceflight affects it, how to take it with equipment available on a spacecraft, and what to do at each level.

Data is stored in SQLite and can be exported as CSV for the medical team. Readings outside plausible physical limits are rejected, so a typing error such as 900 mmHg cannot appear as a critical result.

Benefits

  • Earlier detection. Gradual changes are flagged by trend and escalation rules before they become emergencies.
  • Less reliance on real-time ground support. Communication delays to Mars can reach about 20 minutes each way, so the astronaut needs guidance that works without an immediate reply.
  • Built-in education. Astronauts do not need to be clinicians. Every number comes with an explanation.
  • Motivation. Points, streaks, and badges help people keep up routine checks during long, isolated missions.
  • Low barrier to deployment. It needs only Python 3 and a browser. There are no runtime dependencies, and it runs in a single container.

Intended impact

The tool is designed to support crew health on missions that go beyond low Earth orbit, including transit to Mars, lunar surface operations, and planetary bases. Its aims are to:

  1. Put self-assessment in the hands of the astronaut, consistent with the challenge’s premise that crew must assess their own health.
  2. Make the connection between spaceflight hazards and health visible: microgravity and the heart, confinement and sleep and mood, closed environments and infection risk, and nutrition and metabolism.
  3. Give mission medical teams a structured, exportable record of each crew member’s health history.
  4. Offer a reference design that agencies and commercial spaceflight providers can adapt, with their own approved limits and protocols.

The tool does not diagnose. Its outputs are prompts to act and to contact a flight surgeon, not medical conclusions.

Tools, languages, hardware, and software

  • Backend: Python 3.12, using only the standard library: http.server for the web server, sqlite3 for storage, csv, logging, and unittest for tests.
  • Frontend: HTML5, CSS3 (custom properties, responsive layout, print and reduced-motion support), and vanilla JavaScript. The HTML5 canvas draws trend charts, and inline SVG draws the body map. There are no frameworks and no build step.
  • Database: SQLite in WAL mode, with parameterised queries and explicit transactions.
  • Testing: 40 backend tests (unit, persistence, and HTTP end-to-end), plus browser-level UI tests run with jsdom and Node.js 22.
  • Delivery: Docker (multi-stage-ready image with a non-root user and health check), a Makefile, and a GitHub Actions workflow that runs the tests, builds the image, and smoke-tests the running container.
  • Development environment: Google Antigravity for the initial build, with a prompt included in the repository (ANTIGRAVITY_PROMPT.md) so the project can be rebuilt or extended.
  • Hardware: no special hardware is required. The design assumes off-the-shelf medical devices available on a spacecraft: an automated blood pressure cuff, a fingertip pulse oximeter, a lancet and glucose meter, a digital thermometer, and a sleep log or wearable.

How it is creative

  • The body is the interface. Rather than a list of numbers, a clickable body map links each organ system to its measurements and shows the risk it carries in space.
  • Each reading comes with its next step. Most health apps show a value and a colour. This one tells the astronaut what to do, and when to involve the flight surgeon.
  • Patterns, not just thresholds. The escalation rule catches gradual decline, which is how many spaceflight health changes actually develop.
  • Motivation built into routine. Streaks and points are tied to the routine that protects crew health, not to engagement for its own sake.
  • Designed to teach. The Learn section assumes no medical background and explains why a measurement matters in microgravity, in confinement, and in a closed cabin.

What the team considered

  • Accuracy and safety. Reference ranges are labelled as illustrative. Implausible inputs are rejected. The tool never claims to diagnose, and every critical message points to a flight surgeon.
  • Real constraints of spaceflight. Limited bandwidth and communication delay mean the app works offline on a local server. Equipment is limited to what can fly, so measurements are chosen to match that.
  • Privacy. Logs record only method and path, never health values. Health data is stored locally and can be exported by the crew member.
  • Security. Input validation on every write, a request size limit, path-traversal protection, security headers (Content-Security-Policy and others), and a container that runs as a non-root user. The team documents what is not yet covered: authentication and TLS.
  • Accessibility. Status is conveyed by text as well as colour. The interface supports keyboard navigation, screen readers, reduced motion, high contrast, and touch-sized controls.
  • Maintainability. Reference ranges live in one file, business rules are separate from HTTP handling, and the tests cover the rules, the persistence, and the full user journey.
  • Honesty about scope. The team documented the limits: demo ranges that must be replaced with agency-approved values, in-memory simulation data for the demo, no authentication yet, and plain HTTP until a reverse proxy is added.
